items.stem: In test-driven development, what do you do FIRST when adding a new behaviour?

options.text: Write a failing test that describes the new behaviour
options.rationale: Correct: TDD starts with a failing (red) test before any implementation.

options.text: Write the implementation, then a test to confirm it
options.rationale: That is test-after, not test-driven development.
Refactoring is the last step of the cycle, after the test passes.
Existing tests are kept; TDD adds a new failing test.

items.explanation: Correct: TDD starts with a failing (red) test before any implementation.

items.stem: Which are properties of a good unit test? (Select TWO)

options.text: It runs fast and in isolation from other tests
options.rationale: Correct: fast, isolated tests are central to the F.I.R.S.T. properties.

options.text: It fails for one clear reason
options.rationale: Correct: a focused test points to a single cause when it fails.

options.text: It depends on the order other tests run in
options.rationale: Order dependence makes tests fragile and is undesirable.

options.text: It calls the real external payment API every run
options.rationale: Calling real external services makes tests slow and unreliable; use a double.

items.explanation: Correct: fast, isolated tests are central to the F.I.R.S.T. properties.

items.stem: A test replaces a slow external service with an object that returns canned data so the unit can be tested in isolation. What is this called?

options.rationale: Correct: a stub supplies canned responses to isolate the unit under test.
An adapter is real integration code, not a test double.
Coverage measures executed lines; it is not a test double.
Refactoring changes structure without changing behaviour; it is not a test double.

items.explanation: Correct: a stub supplies canned responses to isolate the unit under test.
